record.paper_title: Current work and open problems in the numerical analysis of Volterra functional equations with vanishing delays
record.original_question: How do the best local superconvergence constants C_m(q) in Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 depend on the proportional-delay parameter q, especially in the limiting regime q 	o 1^-?

evidence.quote: Open Problem 2.2 Analyse the dependence of the (‘best’) error constants Cm(q) in the optimal local superconvergence estimates of Theorems 2.1 and 2.2 on q, especially as q 	o 1−.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the pantograph-type linear delay Volterra functional equations on the interval $I=[0,T]$:

(A) the delay differential equation
$$y'(t)=a(t)\,y(t)+b(t)\,y(qt)+f(t),\qquad t\in I,\quad y(0)=y_0,$$
and

(B) the second-kind Volterra integral equation with proportional vanishing delay
$$y(t)=g(t)+\int_{0}^{qt} K(t,s)\,y(s)\,ds,\qquad t\in I,$$

where $0<q<1$ is a fixed proportional-delay parameter and $a,b,f,g,K$ are given smooth functions.

Let $\Pi_N=\{0=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_N=T\}$ be the uniform mesh of $I$ with stepsize $h=T/N$, and let $S_m^{(d)}(\Pi_N)$ ($d\in\{-1,0\}$) denote the corresponding piecewise polynomial collocation space of degree $m\ge 1$. Choose collocation parameters $0<c_1<\dots<c_m\le 1$ equal to the Gauss(-Legendre) points and let $u_h\in S_m^{(d)}(\Pi_N)$ denote the collocation solution to the relevant equation.

Under standard regularity assumptions, it is known that for each fixed $q\in(0,1)$ there exists a constant $C_m(q)>0$, independent of $h$, such that the following optimal local superconvergence estimate holds at the mesh points:
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\bigl|\,y(t_n)-u_h(t_n)\,\bigr|\;\le\;C_m(q)\,h^{2m},\qquad h\to 0^{+}.$$

Let $C_m(q)$ denote, for each $m\ge 1$ and each $q\in(0,1)$, the smallest such constant for which this estimate is valid (in (A) and respectively in (B)).

Problem. Determine the explicit dependence of the best constants $C_m(q)$ on the proportional-delay parameter $q\in(0,1)$. In particular, analyse the asymptotic behaviour of $C_m(q)$ in the limit $q\to 1^{-}$: find sharp upper and lower bounds, or asymptotic equivalents, describing how $C_m(q)$ behaves as $q\to 1^{-}$ for each fixed $m\ge 1$.
artifact.category_tag: Collocation methods for delay Volterra equations
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent works on optimal superconvergence for collocation methods applied to pantograph-type Volterra equations with proportional vanishing delays (e.g., on uniform and quasi-geometric meshes) establish the $O(h^{2m})$ estimates and discuss the role of the delay function near $t=0$, but a sharp quantitative description of the best constant $C_m(q)$ as a function of $q$, in particular its asymptotic behaviour as $q\to 1^{-}$, does not appear in the located literature. The status is therefore taken as unknown.

status_evidence.title: Optimal superconvergence results for Volterra functional integral equations with proportional vanishing delays
status_evidence.snippet: Analyses optimal superconvergence properties of piecewise polynomial collocation solutions on uniform meshes for Volterra integral equations with multiple proportional delays q_j t.
status_evidence.claim: Establishes optimal O(h^{2m}) superconvergence but does not give sharp dependence of the constant on q as q to 1.

status_evidence.title: Superconvergence in Collocation Methods on Quasi-Graded Meshes for Functional Differential Equations with Vanishing Delays
status_evidence.snippet: Studies optimal orders of superconvergence on quasi-graded meshes for FDEs with vanishing delays.
status_evidence.claim: Addresses orders of superconvergence but not the asymptotics of the best constant C_m(q) as q to 1^-.

status_evidence.title: Current work and open problems in the numerical analysis of Volterra functional equations with vanishing delays
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys results and lists open problems on superconvergence of collocation methods for Volterra equations with vanishing delays.
status_evidence.claim: Lists analysis of dependence of C_m(q) on q (especially q to 1^-) as an open problem.
